extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of poetry, and general readers interested in prosody
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and identify the rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables (meter) in English verse, including major types (accentual-syllabic, falling, rising) and example feet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter
rubrics_metrics.description: The rhythmical pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The predominant meter in English poetry is accentual-syllabic. See also accentual meter, syllabic meter, and quantitative meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accentual-syllabic meter (predominant in English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accentual-syllabic is identified as the predominant meter in English poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as the main organizing principle for English verse; related systems to compare include accentual, syllabic, and quantitative meters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falling meter
rubrics_metrics.description: Falling meter refers to trochees and dactyls (i.e., a stressed syllable followed by one or two unstressed syllables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of feet that produce a falling rhythm are the trochee (stressed + unstressed) and the dactyl (stressed + two unstressed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rising meter
rubrics_metrics.description: Iambs and anapests (i.e., one or two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed one) are called rising meter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of feet that produce a rising rhythm are the iamb (unstressed + stressed) and the anapest (two unstressed + stressed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foot
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The basic repeated unit of meter (a 'foot') underlies the categories above; consult foot for definitions of iamb, trochee, dactyl, anapest, etc.
